nota.t: Biodiversity
Biodiversity is the variety of living things.
Animals: vertebrates (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals) and invertebrates. Flowering plants: monocots and dicots.
A dichotomous key classifies organisms step by step.
1.1 Diversity of Organisms

Biodiversity is the variety of life on Earth: species, genetic and ecosystem diversity. Malaysia's rainforests, mangroves and coral reefs are rich in biodiversity, which gives food, medicine, raw materials and balance in nature.
1.2 Classification of Organisms

Organisms are classified by shared features. Animals are vertebrates (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals) or invertebrates. Plants are flowering (monocots and dicots) or non-flowering (ferns, mosses, conifers). A dichotomous key helps identify organisms.
Ecosystem
Producer → primary → secondary → tertiary consumer; decomposers recycle nutrients.
Interactions: mutualism (+/+), commensalism (+/0), parasitism (+/−), predator-prey.
2.1 Energy Flow in Ecosystems
Energy flows through food chains and webs from producers to primary, secondary and tertiary consumers. Only about 10% of energy passes to the next trophic level; the rest is lost as heat.
2.2 Interactions and Nutrient Cycles

Organisms interact by predation, competition and symbiosis: mutualism (bees and flowers), commensalism (remora and shark) and parasitism (flea and dog). Nutrients are recycled in the carbon, oxygen and water cycles, with decomposers returning nutrients to the soil.
2.3 Conserving Ecosystems
Logging, development, pollution and poaching upset nature's balance. It is conserved through replanting, forest reserves, national parks, biological control, wildlife laws and recycling.
Food classes
Carbohydrates, protein, fat, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water.
Digestive system
Mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine (absorbs) → large intestine (absorbs water) → rectum → anus.
3.1 Food Classes
The seven food classes: carbohydrates (energy), proteins (growth and repair), fats (stored energy, insulation), vitamins and minerals (health), fibre (prevents constipation) and water.

nota.t: 3.2 A Balanced Diet
A balanced diet has every food class in the right amount for a person's age, sex, size and activity. Deficiencies cause kwashiorkor, scurvy, anaemia and goitre; excess fat and sugar cause obesity.
3.3 The Digestive System

Digestion: mouth (salivary amylase breaks down starch), oesophagus (peristalsis), stomach (pepsin in acid digests protein), small intestine (complete digestion and absorption through villi), large intestine (water reabsorbed) and rectum.

nota.t: Disease
Infectious diseases come from pathogens: viruses, bacteria, fungi, protozoa; spread by vectors, air, water and contact.
Immunity
Active (body makes antibodies) or passive (antibodies given); natural or artificial.
4.1 Infectious and Non-infectious Diseases

Infectious diseases are caused by pathogens and spread by air, water, food, touch and vectors such as mosquitoes. Non-infectious diseases (diabetes, high blood pressure, cancer) do not spread and are linked to lifestyle and genes.
4.2 Body Defence

The body has three lines of defence: skin and mucus; white blood cells that engulf pathogens (phagocytosis); antibodies made by lymphocytes. Active immunity comes from infection or vaccines; passive immunity from a mother's antibodies or antiserum.
Water
Water: H₂O, boils at 100 °C, freezes at 0 °C.
Solutions
Solute + solvent = solution. Dissolving is faster with heat, stirring and smaller particles.
Water treatment: sedimentation, filtration, chlorination.
5.1 Properties of Water

Pure water is colourless and odourless, freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C. Impurities lower the freezing point and raise the boiling point. Electrolysis of water gives twice as much hydrogen as oxygen, showing the formula H₂O.
5.2 Solutions and Solubility
A solution is a solute dissolved in a solvent. Solutions can be dilute, concentrated or saturated. Solubility rises with temperature, stirring and smaller particles. Water is the universal solvent.

v.c: Factors affecting the rate of dissolving

nota.t: 5.3 Water Purification

Water is purified by sedimentation, filtration, distillation, boiling and chlorination. A treatment plant uses aeration, coagulation, sedimentation, filtration, chlorination, fluoridation and pH adjustment.
The pH scale
pH 0–6 acid, 7 neutral, 8–14 alkali.
Acid: blue litmus → red. Alkali: red litmus → blue.
Neutralisation: acid + alkali → salt + water.
6.1 Properties of Acids and Alkalis
Acids taste sour, have pH below 7, turn blue litmus red and react with reactive metals to give hydrogen. Alkalis taste bitter, feel slippery, have pH above 7 and turn red litmus blue.
6.2 Neutralisation
Neutralisation: acid + alkali → salt + water. Uses: antacids for gastric pain, slaked lime for acidic soil, toothpaste against mouth acid.
HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O
Electricity
V = IR (Ohm's law).
Series: same current. Parallel: same voltage.
Magnetism
Like poles repel, unlike poles attract.
7.1 Static Electricity and Current
Static electricity forms when electrons move between rubbed materials; like charges repel and unlike charges attract. Electric current is the flow of charge, I = Q/t.
7.2 Current, Voltage and Resistance

Voltage pushes current through a resistance: V = IR (Ohm's law). In series circuits the current is the same everywhere and R = R₁ + R₂; in parallel circuits the voltage is the same on each branch and 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂.
Example: 6 Ω and 3 Ω. Series 9 Ω; parallel 2 Ω.
7.3 Magnetism
Magnets have north and south poles; like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Magnetic fields are shown with iron filings or compasses.
7.4 Electromagnets
An electromagnet is a coil carrying current around a soft iron core. It is stronger with more current and more turns, and is used in electric bells, cranes and relays.
Forces
Force is measured in newtons (N). Weight = mass × g.
Moment = force × distance from pivot. Pressure = force ÷ area.
8.1 Forces
A force is a push or pull measured in newtons with a spring balance. Types: weight, friction, normal force, tension, buoyancy and elastic force. Weight W = mg.
Example: mass 5 kg → weight 50 N on Earth (g = 10 N/kg).
8.2 Effects of Forces
Forces change an object's shape, size, direction, speed and position.
8.3 Levers and Moments
Moment of a force = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot. In balance, clockwise moments equal anticlockwise moments. Levers: scissors, see-saws and wheelbarrows.
Example: 200 N at 1.5 m balances F at 2 m → F = 150 N.
Heat
Heat is energy (joules); temperature is how hot something is (kelvin, °C).
Conduction, convection, radiation. Materials expand when hot and contract when cold.
9.1 Heat and Temperature
Heat is energy moving from hot to cold objects, measured in joules. Temperature is the degree of hotness, measured in °C or kelvin with a thermometer.
9.2 Heat Transfer

Heat moves by conduction (through solids), convection (through fluids, e.g. sea breeze) and radiation (no medium, e.g. the Sun). Black dull surfaces absorb and emit heat well; shiny white surfaces reflect it.
9.3 Expansion and Contraction

Matter expands when heated and contracts when cooled because particles vibrate more and move apart. Uses: gaps in railway tracks and bridges, liquid thermometers, bimetallic strips. Water expands when it freezes.
Sound
Sound is a longitudinal wave, needs a medium; fastest in solids.
Loudness ↔ amplitude; pitch ↔ frequency. Human hearing 20 Hz–20 000 Hz.
10.1 Characteristics of Sound

Sound is made by vibrations and travels as longitudinal waves through solids, liquids and gases but not a vacuum. Loudness depends on amplitude; pitch depends on frequency. Humans hear 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz.
Example: f = 500 Hz, λ = 0.68 m → v = 340 m/s.
10.2 Sound Phenomena
Reflected sound makes echoes. Hard surfaces reflect sound and soft surfaces absorb it. Uses: sonar, ultrasound scans and bat echolocation.
Example: echo after 2 s, speed in water 1 500 m/s → depth = 1 500 m.
Stars
Stars form in nebulae; energy from nuclear fusion.
Galaxies: spiral, elliptical, irregular. We live in the Milky Way.
11.1 Stars
Stars are balls of hot gas producing energy by nuclear fusion. The Sun is the nearest star. Stars form in nebulae and end as white dwarfs, neutron stars or black holes depending on their mass.

v.c: The life cycle of a star

nota.t: 11.2 Galaxies
A galaxy is a group of billions of stars held by gravity. Galaxies may be spiral, elliptical or irregular. Our galaxy, the Milky Way, is a spiral galaxy.
The Solar System
Eight planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
Inner planets are rocky; outer planets are gas giants.
12.1 The Solar System

The Solar System has the Sun and eight planets: the rocky Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars and the gas giants Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Earth lies in the habitable zone where liquid water can exist.
Small objects
Meteoroid → meteor (burns) → meteorite (lands).
Asteroids lie between Mars and Jupiter; comets are ice and dust with tails.
13.1 Meteoroids, Asteroids and Comets

Meteoroids are small rock fragments (meteors when they burn in the atmosphere, meteorites if they land). Asteroids are large rocks, mostly in the belt between Mars and Jupiter. Comets are ice and dust with tails pointing away from the Sun.
